<text style="bold">Guidance:</text> <text style="italic">is the action or the system that continuously computes the reference (desired) position, velocity and acceleration of a vessel to be used by the control system. These data are usually provided to the human operator and the navigation system.</text>

<text style="bold">Navigation</text> is derived from the Latin navis, "<text style="italic">ship</text>," and agere, "<text style="italic">to drive</text>." It originally denoted the art of ship driving, including steering and setting the sails.  This includes planning and execution of safe, timely, and economical operation of ships, underwater vehicles, aircraft, and spacecraft.

<text style="bold">Control: </text><text style="italic">is the action of determining the necessary control forces and moments to be provided by the vessel in order to satisfy a certain control objective.</text>
Generates the desired trajectories (position, velocity and acceleration).

content.content: <text style="bold,italic">The waypoint generator</text>  establishes the desired wayponits according to mission, operator decision, weather, fleet operations, amount of power available <text style="italic">etc.</text>
<text style="bold,italic">The waypoint management system</text> updates the active waypoint based on the current position of the ship.

<text style="bold,italic">The reference computing algorithms</text> generate a smooth feasible trajectory based on a reference model, the ship actual position, amount of power available, and the active way point.
<text style="bold,italic">Sensors</text>  Satellite navigation systems, GPS, radar, gyros, accelerometers,      compass, HPR, <text style="italic">etc.</text>

<text style="bold,italic">Reference frame transformation</text>  translate the motion to that of    the origin of the adopted reference frame.

content: Set-point Regulation, Trajectory Tracking Control or Path Following Control?

content.content: <text style="bold">Set-Point Regulation:</text> The most basic guidance system is a <text style="underline">constant input </text>(<text style="underline">set-point</text>) provided by a human operator. The corresponding controller will then be a regulator. Examples of set-point regulation are constant depth, trim, heel and speed control, etc.

<text style="bold">Trajectory Tracking Control:</text> The objective is for the position and velocity of the vessel to track given desired time-varying position and velocity reference signals. The corresponding feedback controller must then be a trajectory tracking controller. Tracking control can be used for course-changing maneuvers, speed changing, attitude control, etc. An advanced guidance system computes optimal time-varying trajectories from a dynamic model and a predefined control objective. If a constant set-point is used as input to a low-pass filter (<text style="underline">reference model</text>) the outputs of the filter will be smooth time-varying reference trajectories for position, velocity and acceleration (PVA).

<text style="bold">Path Following Control: </text>Follow a path in 3D independent of time (geometric assignment). In addition, a dynamic assignment (speed/acceleration) along the path can be assigned. The corresponding controller is a path following/maneuvering controller.

content: The  task of a ship motion control system consists of making the ship to track/follow a <text style="italic">desired trajectory</text> or <text style="italic">path.</text> Sometimes this also includes motion damping.
In most ship operational conditions, the desired trajectory is slowly varying motion  (LF motion) compared to the oscillatory motion induced by the waves (WF motion).
Due to the motion of ships, motion control problems can have different objectives:

content.content: <text style="bold,italic">Control only the LF motions </text><text style="bold"> (Autopilots, Dynamic Positioning (DP), Position mooring systems)</text>
<text style="bold,italic">Control only the WF motions </text><text style="bold"> (Heave, roll and pitch stabilisation, ride control)</text>
<text style="bold,italic">Control both  (DP with roll and pitch stabilisation in high seas, course keeping and roll stabilisation)</text>
<text style="bold,italic">Wave filter (observer):</text><text style="italic">  Recover slowly varying motion signals from the total measurements</text>
<text style="bold,italic">Controller:  </text>  Generates force commands (desired control action)
<text style="bold,italic">Control allocation:</text>  Translate force commands into actuator commands (RPM, PWR, Torque).

content.content: Control objective: Keep position; follow slow changes in set point.
DOF: 1,2,6 (surge, sway and yaw) [pitch and roll can be incorporated in high sea states in offshore rigs]

Model: time-domain model which includes cross-flow drag effects. The Munk moment, which is in the added mass Coriollis-centripetal terms should be added. Alternatively, use current coefficients (experimental data).
Disturbances: Wind, current, mean wave drift and slowly varying wave forces.
Control Objective: Keep heading or course. For course keeping autopilots, positioning control and guidance systems must also be designed (outer loop).
DOF: 2,[4], 6  (sway, roll, yaw) There is strong coupling between sway and yaw which is not convenient to ignore, and roll also affect these modes.
Model: Manoeuvring model; at high speed lift-drag effects are significant. The model can be linearised for control design because the must operate close to equilibrium conditions.
Disturbances: Wind, waves (there must be a wave filter); for a course keeping autopilot, current is also a disturbance.
Control objective: geometric and dynamic conditions for path following, way-point or trajectory tracking.
Model: nonlinear manoeuvring model.
Disturbances: wind, waves, current.
Control objectives: reduce roll and pitch.
Model: linear time-domain model, with viscous corrections for roll.
Disturbances: 1st order wave induced motion; wind, trim variations with speed.
Control objective: reduce the effect of heave motion in different components of the system.
Model: linear time-domain model + nonlinear viscous effects and structural stiffness.
Disturbances: 1st order wave-induced motion, and rapidly-varying 2nd order wave-induced motions
Control objective: keep formation.
Model: time-domain model with <text style="underline">ship-to-ship hydrodynamic interaction if vessels are too close.</text>
Disturbances: waves, wind, current

content.content: 1st-order wave loads (due to wave spectrum) can be modelled using multi-sinces with random phases or filtered white noise (wave spectrum).
Mean wave drift loads can be modelled as a 1st-order Wiener process (1st-order system driven by white noise.)
Current loads can be included using the concept of relative velocity in surge, sway and yaw (in DP current coefficients can also be used)
Wind loads are included using wind coefficient tables.
Wind areas and centroids from digitized GA
For best results experimental data from wind tunnels should be used.
